title: PT Barnum: More Complicated Than You've Heard
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine P.T. Barnum's complicated life and career, prompted by the film The Greatest Showman. They cover his youth in Bethel, Connecticut, his lottery schemes, his newspaper and jail time, his purchase and exhibition of Joice Heth, his plate-spinning promotions, circus ventures, the purchase of Scudder's American Museum and its hoaxes (the Fiji Mermaid, Tom Thumb, Jenny Lind tour), financial ruin and fires, his conversion to abolitionism, politics including sponsoring the Comstock Law in Connecticut, the Barnum & Bailey circus and Jumbo the Elephant, and his death. Ends with a listener email about the Ted Kaczynski insanity defense debate.

segments.title: Opening banter and The Greatest Showman
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, joking about Jerry's top hat, and say the film The Greatest Showman glossed over Barnum's exploitation and complexity.

segments.title: Barnum's early life and first lotteries
segments.summary: Barnum is born in Bethel, Connecticut, to a struggling farming family. He works at a country store, runs a lottery as a teenager using unsold goods as prizes, and later expands other people's lotteries by selling tickets.

segments.title: Newspaper, jail, and marriage
segments.summary: Barnum marries Charity Hallett and starts his own paper, the Herald of Freedom. He is jailed for libel for sixty days, which sells papers. He leaves Connecticut after lotteries are banned and moves to New York City in 1834.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before returning to New York City.

segments.title: Joice Heth exhibition and the automaton hoax
segments.summary: Barnum buys the elderly enslaved woman Joice Heth, promoted as George Washington's nursemaid, and tours her until she dies. He anonymously claims she is an automaton, and after her death sells tickets to a public autopsy that shows she was much younger than claimed.

segments.title: Senor Vivalla, plate spinning, and early circus
segments.summary: Barnum takes on the plate spinner Senor Vivalla, staging a rivalry with Robert's and promoting free performances. He then joins a traveling circus as a ticket seller, with Vivalla as a performer, and later launches his own circus, which repeatedly fails.

segments.title: Scudder's American Museum and the Feejee Mermaid
segments.summary: Barnum buys Scudder's American Museum in 1841 and renames it Barnum's American Museum, drawing large crowds at a quarter admission. He promotes the Feejee Mermaid, a fake taxidermy specimen, through invented letters and a fictitious naturalist persona.

segments.title: Tom Thumb and Jenny Lind
segments.summary: Barnum promotes Charles Stratton as General Tom Thumb, and later brings Swedish singer Jenny Lind to America for a touring contract that earned him a large sum. Lind reportedly donated her earnings to Swedish public schools.

segments.title: Bankruptcy, fires, and lecture tours
segments.summary: Barnum loses money on the Jerome Clock Company and goes bankrupt, then his mansion and museum burn. He pawns the museum, recovers it, gives lectures on money getting, and buys exotic animals including a dead whale.

segments.title: Abolitionism, politics, and the Comstock Law
segments.summary: Barnum's views shift during the Civil War, and he becomes an abolitionist and Union supporter, using his museum for speeches and plays. He wins a seat in the Connecticut General Assembly in 1865. Later he becomes mayor of Bridgeport and sponsors the Comstock Law in Connecticut, which banned contraception.

segments.title: Barnum and Bailey, Jumbo, and death
segments.summary: Barnum joins with James A. Bailey and forms the circus that became Barnum and Bailey and later Ringling Brothers. They acquire Jumbo the Elephant, who is killed by a train in 1885. Barnum donates to Tufts, which uses Jumbo as its mascot. Barnum has a stroke during a performance and wished to read his obituary before he died.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Hosts close with personal circus anecdotes and wrap up.
